column3: A patient with known gallstones and mild jaundice is rushed into the emergency department with severe diffuse abdominal pain, nausea and vomiting. The abdomen is tender with some rigidity in its upper part; bowel sounds are present. Pulse 108/min, BP 105/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 32/min. What is the most likely diagnosis?
Severe upper abdominal pain with rigidity, tachycardia and tachypnoea in a jaundiced patient with gallstones indicates acute biliary pancreatitis from a CBD stone.
In this patient with suspected acute pancreatitis, which TWO initial investigations best establish the diagnosis?
Serum lipase or amylase >3 times normal with typical pain makes the diagnosis; CT confirms it when in doubt and later assesses necrosis.
How can acute pancreatitis be confirmed radiologically in this patient?
Contrast-enhanced CT shows a diffusely enlarged, oedematous pancreas with peripancreatic stranding and, after 72 h, any necrosis.
What is the treatment of this patient with severe acute biliary pancreatitis?
Admission to HDU/ICU with fluid resuscitation and analgesia, then ERCP (for cholangitis or persisting obstruction) and cholecystectomy for definitive treatment
Severe biliary pancreatitis needs monitored resuscitation and analgesia; ERCP for cholangitis/obstruction and cholecystectomy on recovery prevent recurrence.

A 33-year-old woman has severe upper abdominal pain with radiation to the back within 24 hours of removing gallstones in the common bile duct by endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP). The pain is eased when she leans forward. She reports some nausea and vomiting but denies any diarrhoea. Jaundice is noted and the epigastric region is tender on palpation. Her blood pressure is 120/80 mmHg, and temperature is 37.3°C. What is the SINGLE most likely reason for her signs and symptoms?
The islets of Langerhans contain several hormone-producing cell types (alpha, beta, delta and PP cells).
A and C are false: amylase is not specific (also raised in perforation, ischaemia) and urinary amylase/clearance ratio is unreliable; lipase is more sensitive and specific.
BCDE
A is false: pancreatic injury is uncommon in blunt trauma; it usually accompanies liver, spleen or duodenal injury, and CECT and ERCP/MRCP define duct damage.
Amylase may be normal with late presentation, hypertriglyceridaemia or acute-on-chronic disease, and its level does not reflect severity.
A is false: pancreatitis follows about 3–5% of ERCPs (more after therapeutic procedures); cardiac surgery, gastrectomy and retained CBD stones are recognised causes.
ADE
Grey Turner's (flank) and Cullen's (periumbilical) bruising occur, and hypocalcaemia may give Trousseau's sign; Courvoisier's and Murphy's signs are biliary.

Establish large-bore intravenous access, cross-match blood and begin cautious (permissive hypotensive) resuscitation
A shocked patient with a pulsatile mass has a ruptured AAA: secure IV access, cross-match and resuscitate to permissive hypotension en route to theatre; CT only if stable.
Lactate dehydrogenase
5-aminosalicylic acid (mesalazine)

A 50-year-old woman with known gallstones presents with severe epigastric pain radiating to the back together with nausea and vomiting. Examination reveals localised epigastric peritonitis and investigations reveal an amylase of 650 IU/L. Which of the following would indicate a poor prognosis in this condition?
Amylase of 650 IU/L
White cell count of 10 × 10⁹/L
Painless progressive jaundice with weight loss and a palpable gallbladder (Courvoisier's law) suggests carcinoma of the pancreatic head.
One point per Glasgow criterion (age >55, WCC >15, glucose >10, urea >16, PaO2 <8 kPa, Ca <2, albumin <32, LDH >600); this patient meets three.
Raised cyst-fluid CEA indicates a mucinous (premalignant) cystic neoplasm; a symptomatic body/tail lesion in a fit patient is treated by distal pancreatectomy.
hernia
Sudden RIF pain on exertion with a tender abdominal wall mass on ultrasound suggests rectus sheath haematoma from inferior epigastric vessel rupture.
Total pancreatectomy removes all endocrine and exocrine tissue, causing brittle diabetes and steatorrhoea needing insulin and enzyme replacement.

A 23-year-old woman presents with epigastric abdominal pain and nausea. She is afebrile with normal vital signs. On laboratory results she has no leukocytosis with normal levels of bilirubin and alkaline phosphatase. The amylase and lipase are elevated. Ultrasound demonstrates gallstones, normal gallbladder wall thickness, no pericholecystic fluid, and a common bile duct of 3 mm. What is the most likely diagnosis?
Periumbilical bruising (Cullen's sign) reflects retroperitoneal haemorrhage, e.g. haemorrhagic pancreatitis; flank bruising is Grey Turner's sign.
gitum
Weight loss with a Virchow node (and a heliotrope rash of paraneoplastic dermatomyositis) suggests gastric cancer; endoscopy with biopsy confirms it.

An obese woman with a strangulated paraumbilical hernia causing small bowel obstruction undergoes emergency surgery, and a segment of gangrenous small bowel is resected. What is the best surgical option for the hernia now, and why?
Herniotomy with suture repair (herniorrhaphy); mesh avoided because of the high infection risk in a contaminated field
After resecting gangrenous bowel the field is contaminated, so a sutured repair is preferred; a permanent synthetic mesh carries a high infection risk.
Essay case sequence lost its scenario; logical order is hernia-0002, 0003, 0004, then 0001. Stems rewritten to stand alone.
An obese middle-aged woman presents with a reducible swelling just above the umbilicus that has slowly enlarged over several months. What is the cause of this mass?
Paraumbilical hernia due to obesity and raised intra-abdominal pressure
A reducible swelling beside the umbilicus in an obese adult is a paraumbilical hernia through the linea alba, promoted by raised intra-abdominal pressure.
Which THREE clinical signs best confirm that this supraumbilical swelling is a paraumbilical hernia?
Palpable lump above the umbilicus, reducibility and an expansile cough impulse
A hernia is a lump that reduces and has an expansile cough impulse; redness and tenderness suggest strangulation rather than confirm a hernia.

The same woman later develops bilious vomiting and central colicky abdominal pain with distension; the hernia is now tense, tender and irreducible. Her X-ray is shown. What is the study, what does it show, and what is the most likely diagnosis?
Dilated central small-bowel loops with air–fluid levels on an erect abdominal film, with a tender irreducible hernia, indicate obstruction from a strangulated paraumbilical hernia.
Moderate hypothyroidism raises anaesthetic risk (hypothermia, hypotension, slow recovery), so elective surgery is postponed until euthyroid.
A femoral hernia (femoral triangle lump in an elderly woman) has a high strangulation risk through its narrow neck, so prompt repair is advised.
A lump below and lateral to the pubic tubercle may be a femoral hernia, saphena varix or node; a Spigelian hernia lies far higher, at the lateral rectus border.
C and D are false: a hernia (e.g. femoral, obturator) can easily be missed, and an inebriated patient may still have serious surgical pathology.
B and C are false: inguinal hernia remains the commonest hernia in women, and a femoral hernia lies below and lateral to the pubic tubercle.
A and B are false: mesh is standard but not mandatory (e.g. Shouldice in selected cases), and Lichtenstein does not have the lowest recurrence of all repairs.
A, B and D are false: mesh may be used selectively in contaminated fields, it acts as a scaffold for tissue ingrowth, and plain polypropylene causes intraperitoneal adhesions.
A, C and E are false: laparoscopic repair is used, femoral hernia risk rises after open inguinal repair, and the femoral vein (not nerve) is at risk.
Incisional hernias never develop more than 2 years after the original surgery.
Laparoscopic mesh repair of incisional hernia has a lower wound infection rate than open mesh repair.
A and B are false: incisional hernias can appear many years later, and Jenkins' 4:1 suture-length rule remains valid (now with small bites).
Sliding hiatal hernia|Hernia of Bochdalek|Hernia of Morgagni|Paraoesophageal hernia|Eventration of the diaphragm
Acute pain and vomiting in an elderly patient with a hiatus hernia suggest an obstructed or volvulised paraoesophageal (rolling) hernia; sliding hernias rarely obstruct.

Laparotomy or laparoscopy and operative repair|Continued NG tube decompression and total parenteral nutrition (TPN)|Thoracotomy or thoracoscopy and operative repair|Endotracheal intubation and ventilatory support|Upper endoscopy
An obstructed paraoesophageal hernia risks strangulation and needs prompt (usually laparoscopic) reduction, sac excision and crural repair after decompression.
Incarcerated direct inguinal hernia|Lymph node with abscess|Femoral artery aneurysm|Incarcerated indirect inguinal hernia|Incarcerated femoral hernia
A tender bulge below the inguinal ligament in an elderly woman with coughing (pneumonia) is an incarcerated femoral hernia.
Non-communicating hydrocele|Inguinal adenitis|Reducible inguinal hernia|Incarcerated inguinal hernia|Undescended testes
An intermittent, reducible inguinal bulge in an infant is an indirect inguinal hernia through a patent processus vaginalis.
Antibiotics|Reassurance that the abnormality will resolve without intervention|Referral to the ED for immediate surgical consultation|Referral for elective surgical repair|Scrotal support
Infant inguinal hernias do not resolve and carry a high incarceration risk, so prompt elective herniotomy is arranged.

Urgent surgical exploration|Systemic antibiotics|Elective surgical repair|Sedation with manual reduction and arrangements for elective surgical repair|Sedation with manual reduction, admission, rehydration, and surgical repair within 24–48 hours
An incarcerated infant hernia without peritonitis is reduced under sedation, then repaired within 24–48 h once oedema settles, as re-incarceration is common.
Necrotic bowel in the sac means its blood supply has been cut off: a strangulated hernia. Irreducible or obstructed hernias have viable contents.
A tense, tender, red, irreducible hernia with obstruction is strangulated: resuscitate and operate urgently; do not attempt reduction or delay for imaging.
paed
Maydl's hernia has two loops (W) in the sac; the intervening intra-abdominal loop may strangulate unseen, so it must be checked at surgery.

A 67-year-old male has a swelling in the right groin that appears and disappears. It lies above and medial to the pubic tubercle and protrudes on coughing. It reappears despite pressure over the deep inguinal ring. What hernia is this most likely to be?
Epigastric hernia|Spigelian hernia|Umbilical hernia|Femoral hernia|Paraumbilical hernia
C
A swelling through the umbilical scar present since birth is a persistent congenital umbilical hernia; paraumbilical hernias are acquired, beside the umbilicus.
Dyspnoea, tachycardia and haemoptysis with a swollen leg 5 days after surgery indicate DVT with pulmonary embolism.
Pancreatic endocrine tumours
Insulinoma|Carcinoid|Gastrinoma|Glucagonoma|Non-functioning tumour|PPoma|Somatostatinoma|VIPoma
Secretory watery diarrhoea unresponsive to treatment with a pancreatic mass is a VIPoma (Verner–Morrison syndrome, pancreatic cholera).
Recurrent faints from fasting hypoglycaemia, with obesity from frequent eating and a small pancreatic mass, suggest an insulinoma.
Diabetes, gallstones and steatorrhoea form the inhibitory triad of a somatostatinoma, usually in the pancreatic head.
Refractory duodenal ulceration with a duodenal wall mass in the gastrinoma triangle indicates a gastrinoma (Zollinger–Ellison syndrome).

A 58-year-old man complains of malaise, bilateral backache, nausea and occasional vomiting for 2 months. Clinically there is nothing significant except for bilateral hydroceles, of which the patient was not aware. Routine blood tests reveal: Hb 10 g/dL, ESR 88, CRP 292, urea 22 mmol/L, creatinine 256 µmol/L, K 6.1 mmol/L, Na 135 mmol/L, Cl 98 mmol/L and HCO₃ 18 mmol/L.
Collapse with an expansile, pulsatile mass above the umbilicus is a ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm until proven otherwise.
Dyspepsia, weight loss, an epigastric mass and a left supraclavicular (Virchow) node indicate gastric carcinoma.
Iron-deficiency (microcytic) anaemia with a right iliac fossa mass in an elderly patient is caecal carcinoma.
Menorrhagia with a knobbly mass arising from the pelvis indicates uterine fibroids (leiomyomas).
A thick-walled fluid collection next to the pancreas in an alcoholic with pancreatitis is a pseudocyst.
Splenomegaly
Rheumatoid arthritis with splenomegaly and neutropenia (low WCC) is Felty's syndrome.
Fever, sore throat, posterior cervical nodes, palatal petechiae and a rash after ampicillin indicate EBV infectious mononucleosis.
A
Periodic fever, anaemia, jaundice and splenomegaly after travel to India suggest malaria.
Tender hepatosplenomegaly, ascites and jaundice with recurrent miscarriage (antiphospholipid syndrome) suggest Budd–Chiari hepatic vein thrombosis.
Gallstones, anaemia, splenomegaly and spherocytes with a negative direct Coombs test indicate hereditary spherocytosis.
Pancreatic tumours
Fasting/exercise-induced faintness and sweating relieved by eating (Whipple's triad) suggests an insulinoma.
Profuse watery diarrhoea with hypokalaemia and dehydration despite negative stool cultures suggests a VIPoma.
Diabetes, weight loss and necrolytic migratory erythema (blistering rash) indicate a glucagonoma.

A 48-year-old woman presents with a long history of foul-smelling, bulky stools that are becoming more frequent and severe. She also reports increased thirst and passing large amounts of dilute urine. On examination, she appears thin and wasted but there is no other abnormality.
E
Steatorrhoea plus diabetes (thirst, polyuria) and weight loss form the inhibitory syndrome of a somatostatinoma.
gitemq-0061
A 12-year-old boy undergoing open excision of an appendix mass secondary to acute appendicitis through an oblique muscle-splitting incision centred on McBurney's point.
The gridiron is an oblique muscle-splitting incision through McBurney's point; the Lanz is a more transverse skin-crease version.
A 28-year-old woman with acute lower abdominal pain from a suspected ruptured ovarian cyst is undergoing a diagnostic procedure to confirm the diagnosis.
A 43-year-old woman undergoing hysterectomy for intermenstrual bleeding secondary to uterine leiomyomas (‘fibroids’).
Epigastric/right-sided pain for 48 h with fever, tachycardia and leucocytosis but no jaundice indicates acute cholecystitis.
Sudden severe pain radiating to the flank and back with faintness in an elderly man is a leaking AAA until proven otherwise; renal colic does not cause collapse.
Three days of LIF pain with low-grade fever suggests sigmoid diverticulitis; adjacent bladder inflammation explains dysuria and urinary blood/protein.
